This study aimed to develop a Scheduling and Duty Management System with AI Application in Absence Handling among Security Personnel at Light Rail Transit for Kaizen Security Agency Corp. to improve the efficiency and accuracy of security personnel scheduling and absence management. The study addressed challenges associated with manual scheduling, including the preparation of bi-weekly duty schedules, monitoring of personnel availability, assignment of rest days, and the identification of suitable relievers when personnel are absent.

The study followed the Rapid Application Development (RAD) model. The system was developed using Python with FastAPI for the backend services, Supabase PostgreSQL for database management, and Flutter for the web, desktop, and mobile applications. The system was designed for administrators, head guards, and security personnel and was evaluated by five (5) IT experts and 211 end users from Kaizen Security Agency Corp.

The system provides bi-weekly schedule generation based on station requirements, shift assignments, personnel availability, rest days, preferred stations, and reliever assignments. It also includes absence handling with an AI-assisted recommendation feature that helps identify suitable replacement personnel based on predefined scheduling rules and personnel information. Other features include schedule viewing, duty assignment management, dashboard monitoring, and reporting.

Evaluation using the ISO/IEC 25010 software quality model resulted in an overall weighted mean of 4.74 interpreted as Highly Acceptable. The findings indicate that the developed system provides an effective and organized approach to managing security personnel schedules and handling absences, while assisting administrators in making appropriate replacement assignments.

CHAPTER I
THE PROBLEM AND ITS BACKGROUND
1.1 Project Context

Workforce scheduling in security operations is a complex process that involves balancing shift requirements, personnel availability, and organizational policies. When not properly managed, it can result in missed shifts, excessive overtime, and employee dissatisfaction, which may negatively affect operations, reduce morale, and lead to financial losses (Hughes, 2024). Many organizations still rely on traditional methods such as spreadsheets, phone calls, and printed schedules; however, these approaches often lead to errors, miscommunication, delays, increased administrative workload, and difficulty in tracking real-time updates. These challenges emphasize the need for more efficient and automated systems to improve personnel scheduling and management. Additionally, unexpected absences due to illness, emergencies, or lack of commitment create sudden staffing gaps, requiring administrators to spend significant time manually adjusting schedules and finding replacements (Dhamrait, 2025).

Advancements in information technology have introduced new solutions to improve workforce scheduling. Artificial Intelligence (AI), in particular, has shown significant potential in optimizing scheduling processes by analyzing multiple variables such as employee availability, workload distribution, and operational requirements. AI-driven scheduling systems can automate complex scheduling tasks, reduce human error, and support better decision-making (Kupunarapu, 2022).
1.2 Objectives of the Study
General Objective:

The primary objective of this study is to develop A Scheduling and Duty Management System with AI Application in Absence Handling for Kaizen Security Agency Corp, which manages security personnel assigned to Light Rail Transit (LRT) stations. The proposed system aims to improve the efficiency of scheduling processes, provide convenient access to duty assignments, and assist administrators in handling employee absences through an AIbased recommendation feature.
Specific Objectives:

1. Design a scheduling system that organizes and balances the workload of security personnel through an automated schedule generation feature that follows each station's required number of personnel and assigned posts per shift, observes rest days, and distributes personnel across stations every rotation cycle.

2. Develop an AI-based absence handling feature that recommends suitable reliever personnel based on availability, current schedule or day-off status, shift and post eligibility, and workload distribution, by screening candidates through system-defined scheduling rules and ranking the qualified candidates with the assistance of artificial intelligence.
3. Test the system to reduce delays in assigning replacement personnel and minimize extended working hours of on-duty security guards.

4. Evaluate the developed web and mobile-based Scheduling and Duty Management System in terms of accessibility, timeliness, and usability of schedule information for administrators and security personnel.
1.3 Scope and Delimitations of the Study
Scope of the Study

This study focuses on the development of a Scheduling and Duty Management System with AI Application in Absence Handling intended for security personnel assigned to Light Rail Transit (LRT) stations under Kaizen Security Agency Corp. The proposed system is developed using Flutter for cross-platform accessibility, providing a desktop and web-based application for administrators and a mobile application for security personnel, while a Python (FastAPI) web service hosted on a cloud platform handles the scheduling logic and a Supabase (PostgreSQL) database is utilized for secure data storage and centralized data access. Artificial intelligence is integrated through the Google Gemini API, which assists in ranking replacement candidates during absence handling. The system aims to improve the process of managing duty schedules, monitoring personnel assignments, and assisting administrators in handling employee absences efficiently

User authentication features: allow authorized users to log in and log out securely using credentials stored in encrypted (hashed) form, which cannot be retrieved and can only be reset by an administrator. It implements role-based access control with three roles — administrators, who manage schedules and system data; head guards, who monitor and report the attendance of personnel in their station; and security personnel, who view their assigned schedules and duty information.

Station and post configuration: allows administrators to register stations and define, per shift, the required number of personnel and the named post assigned to each slot, together with the duty hours of each post. This configuration determines how many personnel the system deploys to a station and serves as the basis of schedule generation.

Automated schedule generation: the system generates bi-weekly (15-day) duty schedules based on the configured station requirements, assigning regular personnel to their fixed station and shift with scheduled rest days, assigning relievers to cover those rest days, and reassigning personnel to different stations every rotation cycle while considering their preferred stations. Personnel may only be deployed to stations within their own group or an immediately adjacent group. When the available personnel are not enough to fill a requirement, the system does not stop the process; instead, it produces the best possible schedule and records the staffing problem as a note for the administrator to review.

Scheduling management: the system enables administrators to create, edit, delete, publish, and manage bi-weekly duty schedules of security personnel assigned to various stations. Security personnel are able to view their assigned shifts and schedule details through the system only after a schedule has been published.

Schedule viewing interface: displays generated and published schedules by station, period, and shift, showing each personnel's date, duty hours, and assigned post, with color-coded indicators for duty status such as rest days, absences, and covered duties, to make schedule monitoring easier for administrators

Search and filter functions: that allow administrators to search for security personnel by name and filter schedules and records by station, date, shift, and scheduling period. This feature supports efficient schedule management and quick access to relevant information.

Reporting and archiving functions: allow administrators to generate duty schedule reports per station and per period and leave reports for the year, view historical and past schedules, and export or print reports in PDF format on the agency's letterhead with configurable signatories for documentation purposes.

Mobile application for security personnel: through the mobile application, security personnel can view their assigned bi-weekly schedules, shift details such as date, duty hours, station and assigned post, and access their past schedules. Personnel may also file emergency absence requests before their duty begins, file leave requests, request specific day-offs for periods that are not yet scheduled, and indicate their availability to cover duties on their rest days.

Report Absence of Security Personnel: through the mobile application, the head guard can view the assigned bi-weekly schedule, past schedules, shift details such as date, time and station, view the daily roster of their station, and submit an attendance report per shift identifying the personnel who are present and absent. The day head guard files the morning and afternoon shifts while the night head guard files the night shift, and each shift may only be submitted once.

Dashboard interface: provides an overview of important scheduling information. The dashboard displays the total number of security personnel, schedule summaries, and daily absence, on-duty, and availability statistics to assist administrators in monitoring operations.

Absence handling module: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is integrated into the system to assist administrators in identifying suitable replacements for absent security personnel. The system first applies its scheduling rules to remove candidates who are unavailable, already scheduled on that date, also reported absent, or not qualified for the shift or post, then scores the remaining candidates according to station familiarity, personnel type, workload, and declared availability. The AI reviews this screened list and recommends the most suitable replacement with an explanation, and the ranked candidates are presented to the administrator, who makes the final decision. Duties assigned on short notice are automatically adjusted to give the assigned personnel reasonable travel and preparation time, and replacements can no longer be assigned once the duty has already ended.

Leave management module: allows security personnel to file leave requests and administrators to record and approve them, with the system enforcing the allowed duration per leave type, the required filing lead time, the yearly limit, and the waiting period between leaves. Approved leaves automatically exclude the personnel from schedule generation for the covered dates.

In-app notification module: informs security personnel and head guards of schedule updates, decisions on their requests, and duty assignments given to them as replacements, and informs administrators of newly submitted reports and requests.
Delimitations

This study is limited in terms of system features and implementation. The proposed system does not include SMS or email notification functionality due to the need for third-party API integration, which involves additional system configuration, security considerations, and possible subscription or usage-based costs that are beyond the resources and scope of the study. Moreover, implementing such features would increase the complexity of the system by requiring more advanced backend services for real-time message handling. Instead, the system utilizes in-app notifications within the mobile application to inform users of schedule updates. The focus of the study is to develop an efficient scheduling and absence handling system rather than a full-scale communication platform.

The system also does not include biometric, location-based, or automated time-in and time-out recording. Attendance is established through the attendance report submitted by the head guard of each station, and the system does not compute payroll, salaries, or overtime pay. The artificial intelligence component is advisory in nature; it recommends and ranks replacement candidates, but the final assignment is always confirmed by the administrator, and the system remains fully functional using its rule-based ranking when the AI service is unavailable. The mobile application is deployed for Android devices, while the administrative application is deployed for Windows desktop and web browsers. Finally, the study covers only the security personnel of Kaizen Security Agency Corp. assigned to Light Rail Transit (LRT) stations.

1.5 Operational Definition of Terms

Absence Handling refers to a system feature that records when a scheduled security personnel member is unavailable for duty and suggests suitable relievers based on availability, schedule, shift and post eligibility, and workload, for the administrator's approval.

Administrator (Manager) refers to authorized personnel responsible for managing the scheduling system, creating and updating the duty schedules, assigning security guards to stations, and handling absence reports within the system.

Artificial Intelligence refers to the language model service integrated into the system that reviews the list of qualified replacement candidates prepared by the system and recommends the most suitable replacement security guard, together with the reason for the recommendation, when an absence occurs.

Bi-weekly Schedule refers to the work schedule generated by the system that covers a 15-day assignment of security personnel per station, covering the 1st to the 15th and the 16th to the last day of the month.
Cover Offer refers to a declaration submitted by a security personnel indicating their willingness to be assigned duty on a rest day, which raises their ranking among replacement candidates.
Duty refers to the assignment, responsibility, or task given to a security personnel as displayed and managed within the scheduling system.
FastAPI refers to the Python web framework used to build the backend service of the system, which contains the schedule generation logic and provides data to the web and mobile applications.
Flutter refers to the development framework used to build the cross-platform mobile and web application of the proposed system.
Head Guard refers to the security personnel assigned to supervise a station on a twelve-hour duty and who submits the attendance report of the personnel deployed in that station.
Leave refers to an approved absence covering a range of dates during which the security personnel is excluded from schedule generation.
Post refers to the specific station area or responsibility assigned to a security personnel within a shift, such as platform, roving, or head guard, each with its own duty hours.
Preparation Window refers to the automatic adjustment of duty hours applied when a replacement is assigned on short notice, giving the assigned personnel time to travel and report for duty.

Reliever refers to a security personnel whose function is to cover the rest days of regular personnel and who may be suggested by the system to temporarily replace an absent guard based on availability and workload balance
Rotation Cycle refers to the monthly redistribution of security personnel across stations, which considers their preferred stations while keeping a number of familiar personnel in each station.
Scheduling System refers to the developed web, desktop, and mobile application that automates the creation, management, and distribution of security personnel duty schedules.
Security Personnel is a security guard and user of the mobile application who is assigned to LRT stations and can view their schedules and receive updates regarding their duties.
Station Group refers to the division of the LRT stations into three groups along the line, which limits the deployment of security personnel to their own group or an immediately adjacent group.
Supabase refers to the cloud database service used in the system for storing employee records, stations, schedules, requests, and user credentials accessed by the web and mobile applications.

Local Literature

According to Andaya (2025), artificial intelligence adoption in Philippine digital governance shows strong potential but remains limited in research and implementation. However, the study also noted concerns related to employee well-being, job security, and ethical issues. 2.3 Synthesis of the Review of Related Literature and Studies

This section synthesizes the reviewed literature and studies related to scheduling systems, duty management, and the application of artificial intelligence in workforce scheduling. The reviewed studies consistently show that traditional scheduling methods are often inefficient, time-consuming, and prone to human error, particularly in environments that require continuous staffing such as security operations. As a result, many researchers have explored automated and AI-driven scheduling systems to improve efficiency, balance workloads, and reduce administrative burden through the use of optimization techniques, predictive analytics, and data-driven decision-making.

Although existing studies demonstrate the effectiveness of AI in scheduling and workforce management, most of these systems primarily focus on general schedule generation, workforce optimization, and performance monitoring. They often do not fully address real-time absence handling, particularly the intelligent and automated selection of replacement personnel during unexpected absences. In many cases, absence management is still handled manually or through simple rule-based systems, which may lead to delays in identifying suitable replacements and disruptions in operations.

In response to this gap, the proposed study introduces a Scheduling and Duty Management System with AI Application in Absence Handling that extends beyond traditional scheduling functions. The system integrates an AI-based mechanism that analyzes personnel availability, workload distribution, and scheduling constraints to automatically recommend the most suitable replacement personnel when absences occur. By addressing the missing component of intelligent absence handling, the proposed system enhances existing solutions by improving response time, ensuring continuous operations, and reducing workload imbalance among security personnel.

Figure 3 shows how the same duty information moves once the proposed system is in place. The process begins with the administrator, who registers each security personnel into the system and configures the stations, including the number of posts required per shift. Upon registration, the system automatically generates an account for the security personnel, and on first log-in the personnel confirm their preferred stations, which the system later uses in placing them on duty. The system forwards all pending requests and attendance reports to the administrator for a decision, and every decision made, along with every newly published schedule, is returned to the concerned personnel as a notification.

In the event of an absence, the system filters the workforce for personnel who are eligible to take the vacant post and ranks them. The shortlist, together with the details of the absence, is sent to the AI service, which returns a recommendation and the reasons behind it. The ranking is presented to the administrator, who remains the one to approve or change the assignment; should the AI service be unavailable, the rule-based ranking is presented on its own. The administrator may also export the schedule and leave records as a PDF report.

The system applies the hard rules itself before the AI is consulted, because those rules are scheduling law and are not open to interpretation. A candidate is dropped if they are already on duty at that time, if they are absent themselves that day, or if they are not eligible for the post — relievers are never posted to the night shift, and a head guard post can only be filled by a head guard. Whoever survives is scored on how familiar they are with the station, how well their type fits the post, and how light their workload for the period has been, so a guard who has already worked most of the period ranks below one who has not. A guard who volunteered to cover that date is boosted and always sorts above those who did not.

Only the survivors are sent to the AI service, with the context of the absence, and only the top of the ranking is sent. The AI re-ranks that shortlist and returns the reason behind its choice, which the system stores so the same absence is never charged to the service twice and so the recommendation can be traced afterwards. The administrator sees the ranking with the AI's recommendation at the top, can open each candidate's profile to see their contact details and call them, and remains the only one who can give the final approval. If the AI service is unavailable, the rule-based ranking is shown on its own and the process continues.
Once a replacement is assigned, the system rewrites that duty in the schedule to show the new arrangement, records who covered the absence, and notifies the guard who is taking the post.
Figure 6 : DFD Level 2, Security Personnel Management
Figure 6 shows the four processes an administrator works through to bring a guard into the system and keep their record current: registration, profile maintenance, deployment lookup, and status.

Register Security Personnel (Process 2.1):The administrator enters the guard's name, mobile number, email and role — regular, reliever, or head guard — and picks the stations they prefer. The system draws the next value from the counter, builds a personnel ID and a one-time password from it, stores the bcrypt hash in the credential table, and saves the record. The password is shown to the administrator once, to hand over; it is never readable again, only reset. The record is flagged so the guard must change that password and confirm their preferred stations before they reach their dashboard.

Maintain Personnel Profile (Process 2.2): The administrator searches and filters the roster by type, opens a profile, and edits contact details or role. Resetting a password issues a new temporary one and writes its hash to the credential table  the employee record itself only ever holds a mask. This process is also the source the AI reads from: the attributes it ranks a candidate on are the ones kept here.

Deployment & Station Overview (Process 2.3): The guard is actually posted is read, not typed. The system resolves it from the published schedule for the current period, falling back to the monthly rotation placement and only then to the permanent posting on the record. The same lookup drives the headcount shown per station.

Personnel Status & Removal (Process 2.4): Status is derived at the moment it is asked for, never stored as a flag: on duty when there is a duty entry for today, day off when the guard is in a schedule with no entry today, on leave when an approved leave covers today, absent when today's attendance report marks them so, and unassigned when no schedule holds them at all. From here the administrator can also deactivate a guard or delete the record, which removes the login with it.
Figure 7 : DFD Level 2, Schedule Management
Figure 7 decomposes the process the whole system is built around: turning a station setup and a group of guards into a published fifteen-day duty roster.

Set Generation Period & Group (Process 4.1): The administrator picks a start date and a station group, or a single station. Before anything is generated the system refuses two situations by name: a group that already holds a schedule overlapping those dates, and a special assignment that would leave a guard rostered at two stations at once. Both come back as warnings that say which station and which period, not as a generic failure.

Rotate Station Placement (Process 4.2): The monthly rotation places regulars and head guards across the group's stations for the cycle, weighing each guard's preferred stations against where they were last cycle. The result is stored as the cycle's placement and is what makes "assigned station" a starting point rather than a permanent posting.

Generate Duty Roster (Process 4.3): Placement in hand, the generator fills every required post for every shift on each of the fifteen days, binds relievers to the regulars they cover, and honours pinned special assignments. Generation never fails on short staffing: an uncovered post is written as a schedule note naming the station, shift and reason, and the draft is saved unpublished with its duty entries.

Review & Edit Draft Schedule (Process 4.4): The administrator reads the draft alongside its notes, swaps a guard on a post, or adds and removes personnel. Each edit rewrites the affected duty entries and is checked against the same conflict rules the generator used.

Publish Schedule (Process 4.5): Publishing flips the schedule's status and is the moment the roster becomes visible to guards and head guards in the app. Notifications go out to the personnel affected.
Figure 8 : DFD Level 2, AI Absence Handling

Figure 8 shows what happens between a head guard marking someone absent and a replacement standing the post. The division of labour is the point: rules decide who may cover, and only then does the AI rank the survivors.

Detect Absent Security Personnel (Process 7.1): The head guard files the attendance report for their own shift — the day head guard files Morning and Afternoon, the night head guard files Night — marking each guard present or absent. The report is stored unread, which is what raises it on the administrator's notifications. An absence the guard filed in advance and the administrator approved reaches this process the same way.

Filter Available Security Personnel (Process 7.2): Every hard rule is applied here, by code, not by the model. Out go the absent guard themselves, anyone inactive, anyone already on duty somewhere that date, anyone else reported absent that day, and anyone the post's own rules exclude: relievers never cover nights, a night post needs a night regular, a head-guard post needs a head guard. This process also fixes the cover window — the instant the post times out, past which no replacement can be assigned at all, because there is no duty left to stand

Apply Ranking Criteria & AI Review (Process 7.3): What survives is scored 0–100 on station familiarity, type match, and how light the guard's load is this period; a colleague who volunteered to cover that date is boosted and sorts above everyone else. The shortlist then goes to Gemini with the absence reason and each candidate's recent cover load, and the model returns a recommendation, a confidence, a rationale and a runner-up. The answer is stored against the absence with a fingerprint of the shortlist, so re-opening the screen re-uses it and a changed shortlist forces a fresh review. If the AI is unavailable the ranked list still renders — the screen never waits on it.

Assign Replacement (Process 7.4): The administrator calls the guard, and on agreement applies the cover. That single action rewrites the duty entry to show who is covering for whom, stamps the attendance record "replaced by", writes an audit record of the substitution, notifies the chosen guard that their schedule changed, and marks the stored AI review with who was actually assigned — which is the only honest measure of whether the recommendation was any good. Past the cover window the assignment is refused.

3.4.4 Entity Relationship Diagram
Figure 11 : Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD)

Figure 11 illustrates how all eighteen database tables are interconnected to efficiently manage security personnel deployment, duty scheduling, attendance monitoring, leave and absence handling, AI-driven replacement recommendations, and system notifications. The tables are organized according to how frequently they are written, progressing from standing reference data, to a monthly station rotation, to a fortnightly duty schedule, and finally to the daily operational records filed against it.

Reference data is maintained through the stations and employees tables. The stations table stores each guard post location together with its staffing requirements, which are configured separately for the morning, afternoon, and night shifts, and the named posts that must be filled in each. The employees table stores personnel details and classifies each guard as regular, reliever, or head guard, while retaining their permanent station assignment and preferred stations. System access is managed through the users table, which holds administrator accounts with role-based permissions, and the auth_accounts table, which stores hashed credentials separately from personnel records so that passwords are never exposed through employee data. The counters table supplies the sequential identifiers issued to new employees and stations.

Monthly deployment is governed by the rotation_cycles table, which represents one rotation period, and the station_rotation_assignments table, which records the station and group to which each guard is assigned for that cycle. Exceptions to the rotation are stored in the special_assignments table, which holds guards temporarily posted away from their assigned station for a single shift.

The system centers on the schedules table, which records all work duties. Each row represents a fifteen-day roster for a single station and carries its publication status, its rotation cycle, and any staffing gaps reported during generation. Every schedule expands into the duty_assignments table, which records the individual duty of each guard for each day, specifying the assigned post, shift, and working hours, and identifying whether the guard is serving as a reliever or covering for an absent colleague.

Attendance tracking is handled by the attendance_reports table, which records the daily attendance of personnel as filed by the head guard on duty for each station and shift. Absences and time-off are managed through the absence_requests, leave_requests, and special_requests tables, which store the filing, its supporting details, and the administrator's decision, with the leave_requests table additionally enforcing the day limits and cooldown period applied to each leave type. The cover_offers table records guards who volunteer to cover duties on a given date, together with the shifts and stations they are willing to accept. In cases of absence, the ai_suggestions table stores AI-generated replacement recommendations, linking the absent security personnel, the candidates considered, and the suggested replacement to support decision-making, and later records the replacement the administrator actually assigned. The applied decision is preserved in the replacements table, which links the absent personnel, the replacement, and the affected schedule for future reference and auditing purposes. Lastly, system communication is facilitated through the employee_notifications table, which manages alerts and messages sent to personnel regarding schedules, updates, and system activities.

The relationships shown in the figure are of two kinds. Only one is enforced by the database itself, the constraint between the schedules and duty_assignments tables, which guarantees that deleting a schedule also removes the duties belonging to it. All remaining relationships are logical joins resolved by the system when data is retrieved, most notably the employee identifier carried by eleven separate tables.
Use Case Diagram
Figure 12 : Use Case Diagram

Figure 12 illustrates the complete functional architecture of the Scheduling and Duty Management System with AI, encompassing three primary actors: the Admin, Security Personnel, and the Head Guard. The Admin serves as the central authority, holding the broadest set of privileges across the system. Upon logging in, the Admin can manage personnel by registering new security staff accounts — entering basic employee information and assigning station locations — after which the system automatically generates a unique Employee ID and temporary password sent directly to the new employee. The Admin also configures station assignments and employee time preferences, which feeds into the automated scheduling engine that generates optimized bi-weekly duty rosters. Before any schedule becomes active, the Admin reviews and officially approves it, maintaining full control over all staffing decisions. When absences arise, the Admin handles them by reviewing AI-generated replacement recommendations produced by the AI SmartReplace module, editing the schedule accordingly, and finalizing substitutions. At the close of each operational day, the system automatically compiles station-specific and overall summary reports including total personnel headcount and accumulated coverage hours which the Admin uses for official submission to the head department agency.

Security Personnel access the system through a secure login using their assigned Employee ID and password, allowing them to view their current duty assignments, upcoming bi-weekly schedules, designated station, shift times, special instructions, and historical work records. The Head Guard, on the other hand, logs in to monitor both their own schedule and the duty rosters of personnel under their supervision. Their primary function is reporting absences by verifying station attendance and submitting absence reports when a scheduled employee fails to report for duty. This triggers the AI SmartReplace module, which analyzes factors such as employee proximity, workload distribution, availability, and performance history to generate a curated list of replacement candidates with detailed profiles, enabling the Admin to directly contact and confirm a suitable substitute. Once accepted, the system automatically updates the master schedule in real time, ensuring continuous station coverage and accurate records across the entire security operation.

3.8 Ethical Standards and Consideration

The study involves a working agency, its personnel records, and an artificial intelligence service operated by a third party. The researchers therefore observed the following standards throughout the conduct of the study and in the design of the system itself.

Permission and informed consent. Permission to conduct the study was sought from Kaizen Security Agency Corp. before any data was collected. The purpose, scope, and intended use of the study were explained to the security supervisor prior to the interview, and the session was recorded only after consent had been given. The same explanation was given to every respondent of the evaluation.

Voluntary participation. Participation in the interview and in the evaluation was voluntary. Respondents were free to decline any question and to withdraw at any point without consequence to their employment or standing in the agency.

Confidentiality and anonymity. The personnel records used in developing and testing the system are the property of the agency and were used solely for that purpose. Responses to the evaluation instrument are reported in aggregate, and no individual respondent is identified in the manuscript. Illustrations and screenshots presented in the study show only what is necessary to demonstrate a feature.

Compliance with the Data Privacy Act. The handling of personal information in this study observes Republic Act No. 10173, the Data Privacy Act of 2012. Only the data necessary to operate the system is collected — name, contact details, classification, and duty history — and it is used only for scheduling and duty management, which is the purpose for which it was given.

Security of credentials. Passwords are never stored or displayed in readable form. Each credential is stored as a bcrypt hash in a table kept separate from the personnel records, and an administrator may reset a password but cannot read one. Access to the system is controlled by role, so that each user sees only the information their role requires.

Data minimization in the AI feature. Only the shortlist of candidates who have already passed the system’s eligibility rules is submitted to the AI service, and the payload carries job-related attributes and identifiers only — never names, contact details, or any other personal information. The stored review keeps the identifiers and the reasoning so that a recommendation can be traced afterwards.

Human accountability for decisions. The artificial intelligence is advisory. It re-ranks a list the system has already screened, and it neither adds a candidate nor assigns a duty. The administrator makes the final assignment, and the system records who was in fact assigned alongside what the model recommended, so that the recommendation and the decision remain distinguishable. Where the AI is unavailable, the rule-based ranking is presented on its own and the process continues unchanged.

Fairness in the ranking. The criteria on which candidates are scored — station familiarity, personnel type, workload for the period, and declared availability to cover — are job-related and are applied uniformly. Personal characteristics unrelated to duty play no part in the screening or the scoring.

Integrity of records. Past schedules, attendance reports, and applied replacements are retained rather than deleted, so that a past period can be reviewed as it was actually worked and a dispute settled on the record.

Academic honesty. All literature, tools, and third-party libraries used in the study are duly cited and acknowledged. The results reported in Chapter IV are presented as they were obtained, without alteration.

5.1 Summary of Findings

The study successfully developed an Automated Scheduling and Duty Management System for Kaizen Security Agency Corp. to replace its manual, spreadsheet-based process. The system was developed as three integrated components: a Python (FastAPI) web service for scheduling logic, a Supabase (PostgreSQL) database for records, and a Flutter application for administrators (Windows desktop and web) and for head guards and security personnel (Android). Developed under the Rapid Application Development model, all fifteen modules defined in the project scope were completed, tested, and deployed.

Firstly, the system generates complete bi-weekly schedules for all twenty-five stations directly from station configuration. Generation is demand-driven: administrators declare per shift the required personnel count, assigned posts, and duty hours, and the system deploys exactly as configured. Verification confirmed that daily coverage matched required headcounts per shift and post, no guard was double-booked, rest days were observed, primary head guards totaled 156 hours over 15 days, relievers remained within bounded duty ranges, and no reliever was assigned to night shift. A complete 15-day schedule for a station of nineteen posts was generated in a median of 1.7 milliseconds, with all twenty-five stations (7,700 duty assignments) completed in 0.04 seconds. Rotation redistributed personnel between cycles while remaining reproducible, with preferred-station placement maintained at intended shares and familiar personnel retained at each station. The system completes generation even when personnel are insufficient, producing the best possible roster and recording shortfalls as reviewable notes rather than aborting.

Secondly, the system automates screening, scoring, ranking, and notification of replacement candidates. Upon absence reporting, scheduling rules eliminate candidates who are unavailable, already on duty, also absent, or ineligible for the shift or post. Remaining candidates are scored on station familiarity, personnel type, workload, and declared availability, then passed to the language model for re-ranking with explanatory reasoning. The administrator confirms the final assignment. The rule-based ranking remained functional across all tested AI failure paths—no API key, feature disabled, quota exhausted, network timeout, and malformed response—ensuring system utility does not depend on third-party service availability. The AI feature cost is bounded by absence count, with one model request per absence and cached results. Two temporal rules were added during testing: the expired-post refusal prevents replacement for shifts already finished, and the preparation window adjusts short-notice duty hours for travel and preparation time, with notifications stating both adjusted and original hours.

Thirdly, the unbounded telephone-based replacement process was eliminated. Under the manual process, absences were communicated by telephone or failure to appear; administrators reviewed spreadsheets, decided from memory whom to call, and telephoned candidates sequentially, with each refusal restarting the search. The system enables head guards to file attendance reports directly, delivers them to the administrator dashboard immediately, pre-screens ineligible candidates, presents qualified candidates already ranked and explained, and prioritizes guards who declared cover offers for rest days. The administrator confirms rather than negotiates assignments. Extended working hours end when the replacement arrives, not when assigned. The preparation window ensures assigned reporting times are reachable, and the expired-post refusal prevents assignment to shifts already ended. Notifications contain complete duty information—station, post, adjusted duty hours, and reporting time—eliminating verbal relay.

Fourthly, one record serves three clients: the administrator application (Windows desktop and web) and the mobile application (Android) access the same data through one web service with role-based access. Guards access assigned bi-weekly schedules, past schedules, and duty details directly on their devices without requesting files or visiting offices. Information reaches recipients upon change rather than at next file distribution. Duty status is computed against the server clock in Manila time, ensuring displayed information reflects the current moment. Schedules are presented through station, period, and shift views with color-coded indicators for rest days, absences, and covered duties. Personnel are searchable by name, with records filterable by station, date, shift, and period. Duty reports per station and per period, along with yearly leave reports, are exportable to PDF on agency letterhead with configurable signatories.

Lastly. the system was verified by 284 automated unit checks across twelve harnesses covering generation, placement, rotation, leave, replacement, special assignment, station rename, server clock, and AI modules, all of which passed. Integration testing used a golden-file contract test over fifty-eight read endpoints; all endpoints answered, none were added or lost, and no read fields disappeared. System testing against the deployed cloud service returned HTTP 200 for every requested endpoint, serving 573 personnel records, 25 stations, and 25 schedules over HTTPS. Eleven defects were logged during development; ten are resolved and one remains open—a cosmetic 2.6-pixel tab bar overflow at window widths of 1280 pixels and below, affecting no data or scheduling decisions.

In conclusion, the system has proven to be a complete, efficient, and reliable platform that automates scheduling generation, strengthens absence handling through AI-assisted ranking, reduces administrative delay, and ensures timely information delivery to all personnel, making it fit for operational use at Kaizen Security Agency Corp.
5.2 Conclusion

As the development of the Scheduling and Duty Management System with AI Application in Absence Handling, the project has demonstrated its effectiveness in improving security personnel operations at Kaizen Security Agency Corp. through automation and the integration of demand-driven schedule generation, AI-assisted replacement ranking, and real-time notification mechanisms. The system provides automated bi-weekly roster generation, intelligent absence handling with rule-based fallback, and timely duty information delivery across desktop, web, and mobile platforms, thereby supporting efficient workforce management, reduced administrative delay, and continuous station coverage.

The manual preparation of bi-weekly duty schedules is not a problem of effort but of arithmetic, and the arithmetic is now performed by the system. The challenges administrators encountered in organising and balancing workload — differing requirements per station and per shift, rest days that must be honoured, relievers who must cover them, and a rotation that must move personnel without disregarding their preferences — are all consequences of holding many constraints in the head at once while filling a spreadsheet. The study concludes that when the station configuration itself is made the input to generation, a complete and rule-compliant 15-day roster for twenty-five stations is produced in a fraction of a second, and the administrator’s remaining work is to review it rather than to construct it. The first specific objective was therefore attained.

A scheduling system is trustworthy not because it always fills every post, but because it never hides an empty one. The study concludes that the decision to complete generation and record shortfalls as reviewable notes, rather than to abort when personnel are insufficient, is what makes the generated schedule usable in an agency that is periodically short of guards. An unexplained hole in a roster is a defect; a reported one is information the administrator needs before the day of duty. This conclusion is offered as a design principle for scheduling systems generally, not only for this one.

The delay in handling absences was caused by the search and the negotiation, not by the decision, and it is the search and the negotiation that the system removes. The study concludes that separating a rule-based screening stage from an AI ranking stage answers the second and third objectives together: the rules guarantee that no ineligible candidate ever reaches the administrator, and the AI orders the survivors and explains the order. The administrator’s task becomes a confirmation rather than an open-ended sequence of telephone calls, and because guards may declare in advance their willingness to cover a rest day, the refusal loop is removed for those who have volunteered.

Artificial intelligence is safest in this domain when it is placed where it can only improve an answer that already exists. Because the language model re-ranks a list the system’s own rules produced, the system continues to deliver qualified, ranked candidates when the model is unreachable, out of quota, disabled, or malformed in its reply. The study concludes that the advisory placement of AI defined in Chapter I is not a limitation accepted for safety’s sake alone, but the arrangement that makes the feature dependable for an agency whose stations must be covered whether or not an external service answers that afternoon.

Reducing the extension of an on-duty guard’s shift is a problem of reachability, not of assignment speed. The study concludes that assigning a replacement quickly accomplishes nothing if the reporting time given cannot be met, and that the preparation window — an automatic adjustment of duty hours for travel and preparation, with both the adjusted hours and the post’s own hours stated in the notification — is the mechanism by which the third objective is actually served. The corresponding refusal to assign a replacement to a post whose duty has already ended closes the same problem from the other direction.
5.3 Recommendation
Based on the outcomes and insights from the capstone project, the following recommendations are offered to further improve the system’s performance, efficiency, and impact:
1. Formalize Administrative Protocols and Data Integrity

Establish clear procedures requiring administrators to rename stations only through the Edit Station function, review generation notes before publishing, and confirm all AI recommendations. Provide head guards with orientation on attendance report scope rules to prevent submission errors.
2. Resolve Technical Defects and Infrastructure Limitations

Close the outstanding Notifications tab layout defect at narrow window widths, provision a dedicated staging database for write-path test suites, and eliminate the web service cold start through scheduled keep-warm requests or a non-idling hosting tier.
3. Expand Notification Channels and Platform Reach

Add SMS or email notifications to reach personnel for short-notice covers when the application is not open. Extend mobile support to iOS and implement offline schedule caching for guards on duty without data connectivity.
4. Enhance System Intelligence and Maintain Test Contracts

Analyze recorded administrator decisions against AI recommendations to measure usefulness and refine rule-based scoring weights. Maintain the golden-file contract test by running it before every release and documenting any endpoint differences in writing.
5. Guide Future Research on Long-Term and Cross-Domain Impact

Future Researcher should evaluate longitudinal effects on absenteeism, overtime, and personnel satisfaction over months of live operation. Compare AI and rule-based rankings under live conditions, test demand-driven scheduling in other industries, and examine ethical perceptions of AI-assisted workforce assignment.

USER MANUAL
Logging In
Open Sched - the desktop app on the administrator's computer, or the mobile app on a guard's phone.
Enter the username and password issued to you when your account was registered.
Select Log In. Sched opens the workspace for your role: Administrator, Head Guard, or Security Guard.
Changing Your Password on First Login
Log in using the password the administrator gave you. Sched goes straight to the password change screen — this step cannot be skipped.
Enter a new password of at least 8 characters, then re-enter it to confirm.
Save. A guard continues to station selection; an administrator lands on the dashboard.
Choosing Your Station on First Login
After the password change, Sched shows the list of stations.
Select the station you are permanently posted to.
Confirm. Your dashboard opens.
Administrator
Reading the Dashboard
Select Dashboard in the sidebar.
Read the summary cards across the top for today's headcount — personnel on duty, available, and absent.
Use the duty card to see who is posted right now; the clock follows the server's Manila time, not the computer's clock.
Select any summary card to open the full list behind it.
Viewing Available Personnel
From the dashboard, open the Available summary card.
Review the list of guards who are not on duty, not absent, and not on leave for the selected day.
Select a name to open that employee's record.
Reviewing Absent Personnel
From the dashboard, open the Absent summary card.
Review each absent guard, the station and shift they were assigned to, and whether a replacement has been found.
Note any post left uncovered that is what Procedure 1.04 fixes.
Finding a Replacement for an Absent Guard
From the absent list — or from the prompt Sched shows when a guard is marked absent — select Find Replacement.
Review the candidates. Sched has already filtered out anyone ineligible and ranked the rest by suitability for that post and shift.
Select the guard you want and confirm the assignment.
The replacement is notified in their app, and the schedule for that day updates.
Registering an Employee
Select Security Management in the sidebar, then Add Employee.
Enter the employee's Name and Mobile No.
Choose the Role: Regular Employee, Reliever Employee, or Head Guard.
Enter an Email if there is one — this field is optional.
Select the Preferred Station(s) the employee should normally be posted to. You may leave this empty if they have no preference.
Select Done to register the employee.
Handing Over the Login Details
After registration, Sched shows the Employee Registered dialog with the new username and password.
Write down or copy both, and give them to the employee.
Select Done.
Opening an Employee Record
Open Security Management.
Find the employee using the search box or by browsing the role groups — Regular, Reliever, and Head Guard are color-coded.
Select the employee's row to open the employee detail page.
From the employee detail page, you can perform the following actions:

Reset Password: Select Reset beside the password field, then confirm by selecting Reset on the Reset password? prompt. Sched will display the new password once in the New password dialog. Provide the new password to the employee, then select Done.
Delete Employee: Select Delete Employee, review the confirmation prompt, then select Delete to remove the employee.
Editing Employee Information
Open the employee's detail page
Select Edit.
Update the details that changed — name, mobile number, email, role, or preferred station.
Select Save. Sched confirms with "Employee updated successfully".
Viewing an Employee's Schedule
Open the employee's detail page.
Select View Schedule.
Review their duties for the period — dates, shifts, stations, and posts, including any cover duties they picked up.
Setting an Employee On Leave
Open the employee's detail page.
Select Set On Leave.
Choose the leave type and the start and end dates.
Confirm. The employee is excluded from scheduling for those dates.
Setting the Posts for Each Shift
In the station dialog, work down the shift cards one at a time.
Select Add Post to add a slot to that shift; repeat until the number of slots matches the manning required.
Select a slot to name it — type the post name and select Set.
Clear the footer warning that reads "N post(s) unnamed" before saving, so every slot has a name guards will recognise.
Save the station.
Reviewing a Station's Roster
Open Station Management and select the station.
Review the posts per shift and the personnel currently attached to the station.
Compare the required number against the roster to spot a station that is short-handed before you generate.
Creating a Special Assignment
Open Station Management and open the row menu for the station.
Select Special Assignments.
Add the assignment — the guard, the dates, and the shift it covers.
Save. The assignment is respected when schedules are generated for that period.
Viewing Schedules by Period
Select Schedule Management in the sidebar.
Choose the period you want to look at.
Review the schedules listed for that period, and which of them are published.
Opening a Schedule's Details
From the schedule list, select the schedule.
Review the assignments day by day — station, shift, post, and the guard filling it.
Check any generation notes attached to the schedule

Open Schedule Management and select the period.
Review the schedules you are about to release.
Select Publish All.

Open Schedule Management and select the period.
Select the schedule, or tick several to remove them together.
Select Delete and confirm on the Delete Schedule prompt.

Choose the target: By Group to cover every station in one group, or a single station on its own.
Select the station group — each group covers a range of stations, shown beside its name.
Set the Start Date, check the period length. If it does not match the required number of days, the generate button reads "Fix Schedule Period First" until you correct it.
Click the generate schedule button.

Open the AI review panel shown with the generated preview.
Read the summary of how the period was staffed and any issues it flags.

Select Pick an upcoming duty and choose the duty you will miss. Use Change if you picked the wrong one.
Enter a short reason — for example, "Sudden high fever".
Add the details: what happened, and whether you expect to return for your next duty.
Submit. The request goes to the administrator, and you will see the outcome in your Alerts tab.
Requesting Days Off
From the dashboard, open the special request card.
Choose the days off you are requesting.
Give your reason and submit.
An approved request is taken into account when the schedule for those dates is generated — so file it before the period is generated, not after.
Filing a Leave Request
From the dashboard, open the leave request card.
Choose the Type of leave. Sched shows how many days that type allows.
Enter a Title and a Description, and set the dates.
Submit. Track the outcome in your Alerts tab.
Volunteering to Cover a Duty
Open the Schedule tab and select a rest day.
Open the cover availability screen for that day.
Confirm that you are available. Your name now appears to the administrator when they look for a replacement.
Checking Your Alerts
Open the Alerts tab.
Read your notifications — request outcomes, cover assignments, and schedule changes.
Select an alert to open the duty or request it refers to.
Viewing Your Profile
Open the Profile tab.
Check your details — name, role, and permanent station.
From here you can change your password (Procedure 0.04) or log out (Procedure 0.05).
Filing the Attendance Report for Head Guard
Open the Report tab.
Select the shift you are filing for.
Go down the list and mark anyone who did not report by tapping their row — a guard is Present by default and toggles to Absent.
Check the Present, Absent, and Total counts at the bottom against what you see on the ground.
Select Submit [shift] Report and confirm on the prompt.
When the Submit Button Is Locked
The button tells you why it is disabled. Match the label to the cause:

rows: You already filed this shift. A shift can only be reported once — tell the administrator if something needs correcting.
You are not on duty for this shift. Only the head guard on post files the report.
It is too early or too late. File the report during the shift itself.
